chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali from his father from Ibn Abi Umayr from Hammad from al-Halabi from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a person in ihram who is compelled (by hunger) and finds a carcass (dead animal not slaughtered ritually) and game (caught meat), which of the two should he eat? He said: He should eat the game. I said: Does he not like to eat from his own wealth (to compensate)? He said: The compensation is upon him, so let him eat and let him pay the compensation.

key_terms.الْمُحْرِمُ: The pilgrim in the state of ihram

ai.seo_question: What should a pilgrim in ihram eat if forced by hunger: a carcass or game, and is compensation required?
ai.summary: In this hadith from al-Istibsar, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that a pilgrim in ihram forced by necessity to eat meat should prefer game (saiyd) over a carcass (meitah), as game is inherently permissible but requires fidyah, whereas eating the carcass is also valid but may carry different jurisprudential nuances regarding the obligation of compensation. This ruling highlights the Shia scholarly distinction between the intrinsic permissibility of the food source and the ritual penalty incurred due to the state of ihram, emphasizing that the preference for game is linked to the requirement of fidyah rather than prohibition. The context reflects the practical application of Quranic verses on ihram restrictions, where necessity (darurah) lifts the prohibition but retains the compensatory duty.
